data.title: Modules
data.subtitle: CJS runtime require vs ESM static graph and live bindings

cards.meaning: A file with its own scope that explicitly exports some bindings and imports others. That replaces accidental globals with a dependency graph.

cards.front: Where do you see CJS vs ESM?
cards.meaning: CommonJS: classic Node (require / module.exports) and many compiled Nest/TS backends. ES Modules: browsers, modern Node, what you write in React/RN source, and what bundlers prefer to analyze.

cards.front: When does require() resolve and run, and what does the cache return?
cards.meaning: At runtime when that line executes — synchronous load, module body runs top-to-bottom, cached module.exports returned on later requires of the same resolved path. require is an ordinary call, so it can be conditional or a computed path — a bundler cannot always prove which files are needed.
cards.example: const math = require('./math'); if (cond) require('./a'); require(somehowGetPath());

cards.front: exports.foo = 1 after module.exports = function() {}? What is wrong with exports = ...?
cards.meaning: exports is only an alias to module.exports initially. Replacing module.exports leaves exports pointing at the old object, so later exports.foo does not update what require returns. exports = ... breaks the alias; use module.exports = ... to replace the export.
cards.notes: Use module.exports = ... to replace; exports.foo = 1 is only safe while exports still points at module.exports.

cards.front: Are static import/export runtime calls — when do they resolve?
cards.meaning: No — they are declarations (except dynamic import()). Specifiers are static strings. Parse/link time: build a dependency graph, link live bindings, evaluate in post-order (dependencies first). Static imports are hoisted and run before the module body; the graph is known up front.
cards.example: import main, { add } from './math.mjs'; export function add() {}

cards.meaning: Dynamic import() returns a Promise and allows conditional/async loading; static import stays hoisted and analyzable. Specifier can be computed in many environments, but static import remains the default for tree-shaking and splitting.

cards.front: ESM: increment() then read imported count — can you reassign count?
cards.meaning: Importer sees the updated count — imported names are live bindings to the exporter's variables, not a snapshot of a primitive at import time. Reassigning an imported binding is a TypeError; importers get live read-only views.
cards.example: increment(); import { count } — second log is 1.  count = 5; // TypeError

cards.front: const { count, increment } = require(...); increment(); count?
cards.meaning: count is still the initial value — destructuring copied the primitive at require time. CJS gives you the cached module.exports object; read counter.count or put a getter on exports for live reads. If increment does not also assign exports.count, readers of the copied field stay stale.
cards.example: const { count, increment } = require('./counter.cjs'); increment(); count; // still 0

cards.front: state.n++ on an exported object — visible everywhere?
cards.meaning: Yes. Mutating an exported object's properties is visible everywhere because everyone shares the object reference — true in both CJS and ESM.

cards.front: ESM named vs default — and does CJS have a default export?
cards.meaning: Named: export const a = 1. Default: one per module. Import with import f, { a } from './m.mjs'. Named exports map cleanly to tree-shaking. CJS has no first-class default — one module.exports value (module.exports = fn is a fake default). Prefer named exports in new shared libraries unless the ecosystem already uses default (React).
cards.example:
export default function f() {}
module.exports = function f() {}

cards.front: Why is default import from CJS painful?
cards.meaning: CJS has one module.exports value, not a default slot; interop may wrap with .default depending on tsconfig/helpers. Named vs default mismatch drives esModuleInterop / allowSyntheticDefaultImports. Without them, import fs from 'fs' may fail types or runtime; import pkg from 'cjs-pkg' might need pkg.default on some targets.
cards.notes: Interview line: the systems encode public API differently — not that one is “wrong.”

cards.front: CJS vs ESM circular deps — one interview line?
cards.meaning: CJS cycles often return a partial exports object mid-init — assignment order matters; you can read unfinished state. ESM links bindings first; reading an export before its module finishes initializing can throw TDZ-like errors. Both are reasons to avoid deep circular top-level coupling.
cards.example: CJS: b sees a.loaded === false. ESM: export const b = 'b' + a may throw if a is not initialized.

cards.meaning: .mjs always ESM; .cjs always CJS; package.json "type":"module" makes .js ESM; omitted or "type":"commonjs" treats .js as CJS. Don't assume .js is ESM (or CJS) without checking the nearest package.json. Source import syntax ≠ runtime if tsc emits require.

cards.front: Why is CJS harder to tree-shake than ESM?
cards.meaning: require is a runtime call — conditional, dynamic paths, try/catch — a bundler cannot always know used modules without executing code. Static import/export give a build-time usage graph to drop unused exports. Some bundlers heuristically shake simple CJS, but ESM is the model designed for it (lodash-es named imports vs import _ from 'lodash').

cards.front: Nest/TS: you wrote import — still ESM at runtime? __dirname?
cards.meaning: Not necessarily — many Nest apps emit commonjs (require) while source uses import. That affects __dirname, top-level await, and default-import interop; check tsconfig module and package.json type. __dirname / __filename are easy in CJS; in native ESM use import.meta.url.
cards.notes: Stack connection: source syntax ≠ runtime system.

cards.front: Top-level this and top-level await: CJS vs ESM?
cards.meaning: Node CJS wrapper: this is often the exports object (same starting object as module.exports before reassignment). ESM: this is undefined, always strict. ESM can use top-level await in supporting runtimes; CJS cannot at the top level without wrapping in an async IIFE.
